related_questions.question: What is the most common cause of breast cancer?
related_questions.snippet: The exact cause of most breast cancers isn't known. Researchers have found things that increase the risk of breast cancer. These include hormones, lifestyle choices and things in the environment. But it's not clear why some people who don't have any factors get cancer, yet others with risk factors never do.

related_questions.question: What are the five warning signs of breast cancer?

text_blocks.snippet: Five common warning signs of breast cancer include: a new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm area, changes in breast size or shape, skin changes like dimpling or redness, nipple changes such as inversion or discharge, and breast pain. It's crucial to remember that these symptoms can also be caused by other conditions, but any new or concerning changes should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.
snippet_highlighted_words: a new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm area, changes in breast size or shape, skin changes like dimpling or redness, nipple changes such as inversion or discharge, and breast pain

list.title: New lump or thickening:
list.snippet: A new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm area is a common sign, but it's important to note that not all lumps are cancerous. Some are benign cysts or other non-cancerous conditions. However, any new lump should be checked by a doctor.

list.title: Changes in breast size or shape:
list.snippet: Noticeable changes in the size, shape, or contour of one or both breasts can be a warning sign. This could include a breast becoming larger or smaller, or developing an unusual shape.

list.title: Skin changes:
list.snippet: Changes in the skin of the breast, such as dimpling, redness, or thickening, can be a sign. Sometimes the skin may look like an orange peel. It's important to note that these changes can be harder to see on darker skin tones.

list.title: Nipple changes:
list.snippet: Nipple changes, such as an inverted nipple (turned inward), discharge (other than breast milk), or skin changes around the nipple, can be a warning sign. Any new or persistent nipple discharge, especially if it's bloody or occurs without breastfeeding, should be evaluated.

list.title: Breast pain:
list.snippet: While breast pain is common and often not related to cancer, persistent or localized pain in one area of the breast should be checked by a doctor, especially if it's not related to menstrual cycles or other known causes.

text_blocks.snippet: While it's impossible to guarantee prevention of breast cancer, several lifestyle choices can significantly lower the risk. These include maintaining a healthy weight, being physically active, limiting alcohol consumption, not smoking, and potentially breastfeeding. Regular screening is also crucial for early detection.
snippet_highlighted_words: maintaining a healthy weight, being physically active, limiting alcohol consumption, not smoking, and potentially breastfeeding

list.snippet: Maintain a healthy weight: Obesity, particularly after menopause, is linked to increased breast cancer risk.
Be physically active: Regular exercise, aiming for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity per week, is beneficial.
Limit alcohol consumption: Even moderate alcohol intake is associated with an increased risk.
Don't smoke: Smoking is linked to various cancers, including breast cancer.
Consider breastfeeding: If possible, breastfeeding can offer some protective benefits.

list.title: Regular screening:
list.snippet: Mammograms and other screening methods can help detect breast cancer early, when it's most treatable.

list.title: Diet:
list.snippet: A balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, while limiting red meat and processed foods, can contribute to overall health and potentially lower risk.

list.title: Hormone therapy:
list.snippet: Be cautious with hormone replacement therapy (HRT) after menopause, as it can increase risk. Discuss the risks and benefits with a healthcare professional.

list.title: Be aware of risk factors:
list.snippet: Factors like family history, age, and genetics play a role, but you can still take steps to mitigate risk.

list.title: Consult your doctor:
list.snippet: Discuss your individual risk factors and screening recommendations with your healthcare provider.

related_questions.title: Breast Cancer Risk Factors - CDC

text_blocks.snippet: While the exact causes of breast cancer remain unknown, several risk factors have been identified that can increase a person's likelihood of developing the disease. These factors include age, family history of breast cancer, genetic mutations, lifestyle choices, and certain medical conditions.
snippet_highlighted_words: age, family history of breast cancer, genetic mutations, lifestyle choices, and certain medical conditions

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at the risk factors:
Age: The risk of breast cancer increases with age, with most women being diagnosed after age 50.
Family History: Having a close family member (mother, sister, daughter) with breast cancer, especially at a young age, significantly increases the risk.
Genetic Mutations: Certain inherited gene mutations, such as those in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, are strongly linked to an increased risk of breast cancer.

list.title: Alcohol Consumption:
list.snippet: Drinking alcohol is a known risk factor for breast cancer, with the risk increasing with higher alcohol consumption.

list.title: Obesity:
list.snippet: Being overweight or obese, especially after menopause, can increase breast cancer risk.

list.title: Physical Inactivity:
list.snippet: Lack of physical activity has also been linked to an increased risk.

list.title: Hormone Replacement Therapy:
list.snippet: The use of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for more than 5 years can increase the risk.

list.title: Certain Birth Control Pills:
list.snippet: Some studies suggest a link between certain birth control pills and increased breast cancer risk.

list.title: Dense Breasts:
list.snippet: Women with dense breast tissue may have a higher risk.

list.title: Radiation Exposure:
list.snippet: Exposure to radiation, particularly to the chest area during childhood or adolescence, can increase the risk.

list.title: Early Menarche (First Period) or Late Menopause:
list.snippet: Starting menstruation before age 12 or reaching menopause after age 55 can slightly increase risk.

list.title: Never Giving Birth or Giving Birth After Age 30:
list.snippet: Women who have never given birth or had their first child after age 30 have a slightly higher risk.

text_blocks.snippet: Important Note: It's crucial to remember that having risk factors does not guarantee breast cancer development, and many women with breast cancer have no known risk factors. Similarly, not having risk factors does not mean a woman is immune to the disease.
